TargetRLF1: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs), also known as sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), are infections that are typically spread through sexual contact, including vaginal, anal, or oral sex. These infections can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites, and they can have serious health consequences if left untreated. Common STIs include chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, human papillomavirus (HPV), and HIV/AIDS ayo Here are some ways to prevent the transmission of STIs:  Abstinence: The most effective way to prevent STIs is to abstain from sexual activity (vaginal, anal, or oral) with a partner who has an STI or whose STI status is unknown.  Use Condoms: Consistently and correctly using condoms during sexual activity can significantly reduce the risk of STI transmission. Use latex or polyurethane condoms for vaginal or anal sex, and use condoms or dental dams for oral sex.  Limit Sexual Partners: Having fewer sexual partners reduces your risk of exposure to STIs. Mutual monogamy with a partner who has tested negative for STIs can also lower your risk.  Communication: Talk openly and honestly with your sexual partners about STIs, testing, and safer sex practices. Encourage each other to get tested regularly for STIs.  Get Tested: Get tested for STIs regularly, especially if you are sexually active with multiple partners or have had unprotected sex. Many STIs do not cause symptoms, so testing is the only way to know your STI status.  Vaccination: Vaccines are available to prevent certain STIs, such as HPV and hepatitis B. Talk to your healthcare provider about whether vaccination is appropriate for you.  Avoid Sharing Needles: If you use injectable drugs, never share needles or other drug paraphernalia. Sharing needles can transmit STIs such as HIV and hepatitis B and C.  Practice Safer Sex: Avoid high-risk sexual behaviors, such as unprotected sex with multiple partners or engaging in sex while under the influence of drugs or alcohol. Use your best judgment and prioritize your health and safety.  Routine Health Care: Attend regular check-ups with your healthcare provider for sexual health screenings and preventive care. Seek medical attention promptly if you experience symptoms of an STI or have been exposed to an STI.  By practicing safer sex, getting tested regularly, and communicating openly with your sexual partners, you can reduce your risk of contracting STIs and protect your sexual health. If you have questions or concerns about STI prevention, don't hesitate to speak with a healthcare provider or sexual health professional for guidance and support.

TargetRLF1: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) can infect individuals of all blood types, and there is no specific blood group that is more susceptible to HIV infection than others. HIV primarily infects specific immune cells in the body called CD4+ T cells, and it does not have a preference for a particular blood group. HIV is primarily transmitted through contact with certain body fluids, including blood, semen, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids, and breast milk, that contain a high concentration of the virus. It's important to note that HIV does not directly interact with or target the antigens present on the surface of red blood cells, which determine an individual's ABO blood type (e.g., A, B, AB, O). Blood type antigens are not receptors for HIV infection. HIV is a virus that primarily targets the immune system, specifically CD4+ T cells, and over time, it can weaken the immune system, leading to a variety of health problems if left untreated. The risk of HIV infection is related to behaviors and practices that expose individuals to the virus, rather than their blood type.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

You should get tested regularly if you have unprotected sex with a new partner, multiple partners or a partner who has an STI. You should also get tested if you have symptoms or you are pregnant. TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications.. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Your need for testing depends on your personal risk for getting Chlamydia. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample. You should get tested regularly if you have unprotected sex with a new partner, multiple partners or a partner who has an STI. You should also get tested if you have symptoms or you are pregnant. Many people with Chlamydia don't have symptoms. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis develops in stages. The symptoms vary with each stage. But the stages may overlap. And the symptoms don't always happen in the same order. You may be infected with syphilis bacteria without noticing any symptoms for years. Primary syphilis: The first symptom of syphilis is a small sore called a chancre (SHANG-kur) that appears 2-12 weeks after exposure to someone with Syphilis. The sore is often painless. It appears at the spot where the bacteria entered your body. Most people with syphilis develop only one chancre. Some people get more than one. The chancre often forms about three weeks after you come in contact with syphilis bacteria. Many people who have syphilis don't notice the chancre. That's because it's usually painless. It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. It usually starts on the body's trunk, including chest, stomach, pelvis, back, and limbs. In time, it also could appear on the limbs, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Besides the rash, other symptoms may include wartlike sores, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Symptoms of secondary syphilis may go away on their own. But without treatment, they could come and go for months or years. Latent syphilis: If you aren't treated for syphilis, the disease moves from the secondary stage to the latent stage. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Tertiary syphilis: After the latent stage, up to 30% to 40% of people with syphilis who don't get treatment have complications known as tertiary syphilis. Here, they may develop permanently damaged heart, brain, muscles, bones, and eyes. Congenital syphilis: Pregnant people who have syphilis can pass the disease to their babies. Unborn babies can become infected through the organ that provides nutrients and oxygen in the womb, called the placenta. Infection also can happen during birth. Newborns with congenital syphilis might have no symptoms. But without fast treatment, some babies might get sores and rashes on the skin, fever, a type of discolored skin and eyes called jaundice, not enough red blood cells (anemia), swollen spleen and liver, sneezing or a stuffed, drippy nose called rhinitis, bone changes, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

TargetRLF1: PrEP, which stands for Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis, is a preventive approach to reducing the risk of HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) infection in individuals who are at high risk of contracting the virus. PrEP involves taking a daily medication to lower the risk of acquiring HIV. It's important to note that PrEP is not a substitute for safer sex practices or regular HIV testing. Rather, it is an additional tool in the toolkit of HIV prevention. If you are considering PrEP, consult with a healthcare provider who can provide guidance on whether it is an appropriate choice for you and help you develop a comprehensive HIV prevention plan tailored to your needs and circumstances.

TargetRLF1: Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes is a highly contagious disease. It is transmitted from an infected person to the other through direct contact. Herpes simplex-1 (HSV-1) is predominantly oral, therefore it can be transmitted by kissing an infected person, getting in contact with saliva of an infected person and  surfaces which are contaminated with the virus. Herpes simplex-2 (HSV-2) is predominantly ano-genital. Transmission of HSV-2 is by contact through unprotected sexual intercourse. All types of sex including oral sex, anal sex, and vaginal sex can result in the spread of HSV-2. Getting in direct contact with vaginal fluids and herpetic sores also can lead to transmission of the virus.

TargetRLF1: The only way to completely avoid STIs is to not have vaginal, anal, or oral sex. If you are sexually active, you can do the following things to lower your chances of getting Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes:•        Being in a long-term mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who does not have herpes.•        Using condoms the right way every time you have sex.Be aware that not all herpes sores occur in areas that a condom can cover. Also, the skin can release the virus (shed) from areas that do not have a visible herpes sore. For these reasons, condoms may not fully protect you from getting herpes. If your sex partner(s) has/have genital herpes, you can lower your risk of getting it if:•        Your partner takes an anti-herpes medicine every day. This is something your partner should discuss with his or her healthcare provider.•        You avoid having vaginal, anal, or oral sex when your partner has herpes symptoms (i.e., during an "outbreak").If you are pregnant and have genital herpes, prenatal care visits are very important. Some research suggest that a genital herpes infection may lead to miscarriage or make it more likely to deliver your baby too early. You can pass herpes to your unborn child before birth, but it more commonly passes during delivery. This can lead to a deadly infection in your baby (called neonatal herpes). It is important that you avoid getting genital herpes during pregnancy. Tell your healthcare provider if you have ever had a genital herpes diagnosis or symptoms. Also tell them about any possible exposure to genital herpes. If you have genital herpes, you may need to take anti-herpes medicine towards the end of your pregnancy. This medicine may reduce your risk of having signs or symptoms of genital herpes when you deliver. At the time of delivery, your healthcare provider should carefully examine you for herpes sores. If you have signs or symptoms of genital herpes at delivery, a 'C-section' is likely to occur.

TargetRLF1: People with hepatitis B infections present varying symptoms. They stay with positive status for hepatitis B but while asymptomatic. Where as patients who suffer the advanced hepatitis B complications such liver cirrhosis and Hepatocellular carcinoma, they have symptoms and signs of liver disease such as loss of weight, loss of appetite, body swelling, yellowing of eyes among others.

TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). These lesions burn and can be painful. They can appear on the buttocks, anus or thighs, on the vulva or vagina in women, and on the penis or scrotum in men. Often, before the lesions appear, patients describe a prodrome, characterized by a tingling or burning sensation in the area where the lesions will develop that can be noticed during urination, along with itching or discomfort in the genital area. You can also have the following symptoms, Blisters on the mouth or lips, Fever, headache or pain in the joints, Trouble urinating. In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathing, short periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

TargetRLF1: Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as Herpes is caused by two types of herpes simplex virus. The genital infection caused by these two viruses manifests in the same way. Type 1 (HSV-1) mostly spreads by oral contact and causes infections in or around the mouth (oral herpes or cold sores). It can also cause genital herpes. Most adults are infected with HSV-1. Type 2 (HSV-2) spreads by sexual contact and causes genital herpes. However, it is also possible for HSV-2 to cause oral herpes. In rare circumstances, herpes (HSV-1 and HSV-2) can be transmitted from mother to child during delivery, causing neonatal herpes.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis develops in stages. The symptoms vary with each stage. But the stages may overlap. And the symptoms don't always happen in the same order. You may be infected with syphilis bacteria without noticing any symptoms for years. Primary syphilis: The first symptom of syphilis is a small sore called a chancre (SHANG-kur) that appears 2-12 weeks after exposure to someone with Syphilis. The sore is often painless. It appears at the spot where the bacteria entered your body. Most people with syphilis develop only one chancre. Some people get more than one. The chancre often forms about three weeks after you come in contact with syphilis bacteria. Many people who have syphilis don't notice the chancre. That's because it's usually painless. It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. It usually starts on the body's trunk, including chest, stomach, pelvis, back, and limbs. In time, it also could appear on the limbs, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Besides the rash, other symptoms may include wartlike sores, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Symptoms of secondary syphilis may go away on their own. But without treatment, they could come and go for months or years. Latent syphilis: If you aren't treated for syphilis, the disease moves from the secondary stage to the latent stage. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Tertiary syphilis: After the latent stage, up to 30% to 40% of people with syphilis who don't get treatment have complications known as tertiary syphilis. Here, they may develop permanently damaged heart, brain, muscles, bones, and eyes. Congenital syphilis: Pregnant people who have syphilis can pass the disease to their babies. Unborn babies can become infected through the organ that provides nutrients and oxygen in the womb, called the placenta. Infection also can happen during birth. Newborns with congenital syphilis might have no symptoms. But without fast treatment, some babies might get sores and rashes on the skin, fever, a type of discolored skin and eyes called jaundice, not enough red blood cells (anemia), swollen spleen and liver, sneezing or a stuffed, drippy nose called rhinitis, bone changes, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

The organism that causes the disease was first discovered in 1879 in Albert Neisser, hence the organisma being called Neisseria Gonorrhoea. The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

TargetRLF1: Human Immunodeficiency Virus is an infection that originated in animals and passed into human bodies. It came to global attention after doctors started receiving reports of uncommon cases of pneumonia, cancer, and other illnesses in young gay homosexual men and injection drug users. Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Unborn babies can become infected through the organ that provides nutrients and oxygen in the womb, called the placenta. Infection also can happen during birth. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

In those days, men were considered victims and women as the source of the disease. The organism that causes the disease was first discovered in 1879 in Albert Neisser, hence the organisma being called Neisseria Gonorrhoea. The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

TargetRLF1: PEP stands for "Post-Exposure Prophylaxis." It's important to note that PEP is not a substitute for regular HIV prevention methods, such as condom use and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for individuals at ongoing risk of HIV infection. If you believe you have been exposed to HIV, seek medical attention immediately to discuss whether PEP is appropriate for your situation.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

Yafuatayo ni baadhi ya mambo muhimu ya kuzingatia: Tofauti ya Mtu Binafsi, Tiba ya Kudhibiti Virusi vya Ukimwi (ART), Hesabu ya CD4, Mzigo wa Virusi, Kuzingatia Matibabu, Umri na Afya, Sarafu, Sababu za Kinasaba, na Upatikanaji wa Huduma ya Afya. Ni muhimu kusisitiza kwamba kwa utambuzi wa wakati, huduma za matibabu zinazofaa, na kuzingatia ART, watu wengi wanaoishi na virusi vya ukimwi wanaweza kudumisha afya zao na kuishi maisha marefu, yenye ufanisi bila kuendeleza UKIMWI. Uchunguzi wa mara kwa mara wa kimatibabu, idadi ya CD4 na ufuatiliaji wa wingi wa virusi, na mawasiliano ya wazi na watoa huduma za afya ni muhimu ili kudhibiti virusi vya ukimwi kwa ufanisi. Pia ni muhimu kutambua kwamba "UKIMWI" ni hatua maalum ya maambukizi ya virusi vya ukimwi inayojulikana na mfumo dhaifu wa kinga na uwepo wa magonjwa fulani nyemelezi au magonjwa yanayofafanua UKIMWI. Neno "walio na virusi vya ukimwi" linarejelea watu ambao wana virusi lakini sio lazima waendelee na UKIMWI. Uchunguzi wa mapema na matibabu inaweza kusaidia kuzuia kuendelea kwa UKIMWI na matatizo yanayohusiana nayo.
